subject: biology

items.q: A student says: 'Adult barnacles are cemented to rocks and are sessile, so they are an exception to the idea that adaptations for movement are a universal feature of living organisms.' Which is the best response?
items.correct: Barnacles are not an exception: the adult uses muscles to beat its feathery cirri to capture food and to close its shell plates when disturbed.
items.misconception: The student is right: once cemented to the rock the adult barnacle does not move at all, so it has no adaptations for movement.
items.why: The word 'sessile' is introduced as the opposite of 'motile', and in everyday use 'moving' means going somewhere, so students equate not moving from place to place with not moving at all. Sponges, corals and barnacles are also usually met as still photographs. Adaptations for movement are a universal feature of living organisms. A sessile species does not locomote, but it moves parts of its body: the barnacle sweeps the water with muscle-driven cirri, and a sea anemone bends its tentacles towards its mouth. Sessile describes the absence of locomotion, not the absence of movement.
items.specStatementText: Movement is universal, locomotion is not
items.random_wrong: The student is right: the adult barnacle is a passive filter feeder relying on the water current, so movement plays no part in its life.

items.q: Electron micrographs of a sarcomere are taken before and after it contracts. Which set of changes is observed?
items.correct: The sarcomere is shorter; the A band keeps its width while the I band and the H zone are both narrower.
items.misconception: The sarcomere is shorter; the A band, the I band and the H zone are all narrower, each in the same proportion.
items.why: In everyday language to contract means to shrink, and a bulging biceps looks as though something inside is bunching up. Diagrams that show a relaxed and a contracted sarcomere without a scale invite the reading that everything has shrunk in proportion. The sliding filament model states that the filaments keep their length. The evidence is in the banding pattern: the A band, which is the full length of the myosin filaments, does not change; the I band (actin only) and the H zone (myosin only) both narrow because the overlap increases.
items.random_wrong: The sarcomere is shorter; the A band and the H zone keep their width and only the I band is narrower.

items.q: What is the role of ATP in the cross-bridge cycle of muscle contraction?
items.correct: Binding of ATP releases the myosin head from actin, and its hydrolysis re-cocks the head for the next cycle.
items.misconception: ATP is hydrolysed to power the pull of the head on actin; when ATP is used up the heads let go and the muscle relaxes.
items.why: ATP is taught as 'the energy for contraction', and relaxation is imagined as the passive default state that needs no energy. Students have not been told that breaking a cross-bridge is itself an ATP-dependent step. In the cross-bridge cycle, binding of a fresh ATP molecule to the myosin head is what releases the head from actin; hydrolysis of that ATP then re-cocks the head. Without ATP the heads stay bound and the muscle cannot lengthen, which is why rigor mortis develops after death. Relaxation also needs ATP to pump calcium ions back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
items.random_wrong: One ATP is hydrolysed at the start of a contraction; the heads then ratchet along the actin without ever detaching.

items.q: A drug blocks the release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of a skeletal muscle fibre. The motor neuron still stimulates the fibre normally. What is the effect on the fibre?
items.correct: No cross-bridges form, because tropomyosin still covers the myosin-binding sites on actin.
items.misconception: Myosin heads attach to actin but cannot pivot, because calcium ions are needed for the power stroke.
items.why: Calcium is named as 'the trigger for contraction' before troponin and tropomyosin are introduced, and the myosin head is the part that visibly does something in animations, so the trigger is attached to the mover. Calcium ions regulate access, not power. Bound to troponin they shift tropomyosin and uncover the binding sites on actin. The energy comes from ATP hydrolysed by the myosin head, and the pull is produced when the attached head pivots.
items.random_wrong: The fibre contracts normally, because the action potential in its membrane makes the filaments slide directly.

items.q: What are the roles of the protein titin in a sarcomere?
items.correct: It acts as an elastic spring that returns a stretched sarcomere to its resting length and stiffens to stop it being overstretched.
items.misconception: It forms a third set of filaments that shorten actively to help pull the Z lines together during contraction.
items.why: Titin is introduced alongside actin and myosin as another sarcomere protein, and students have just learned that sarcomere proteins produce contraction, so the new protein is slotted into the same role. Titin's roles are in relaxation, not contraction: it helps the sarcomere recoil after stretching and prevents it from being stretched too far. It behaves as a spring, not as a motor.
items.specStatementText: Titin and antagonistic muscles in relaxation
items.random_wrong: It pulls a contracted sarcomere back out to its resting length, so that an antagonistic muscle is not required.

items.q: The biceps contracts and shortens to flex the elbow. When the arm is then straightened, how is the biceps returned to its longer, resting length?
items.correct: Contraction of the triceps moves the forearm, and this pulls the relaxed biceps longer, since a muscle cannot lengthen itself.
items.misconception: The biceps lengthens itself by reversing its cross-bridge cycle, so that the myosin heads push the actin filaments back outwards.
items.why: In everyday life we 'push' with our arms, and the sensation of straightening a limb feels like a push. Students also assume symmetry: if contraction is active, extension must be active too. Every movement, including a push-up, is produced by muscles pulling on bones. A contracted muscle cannot lengthen itself, which is why muscles are arranged in antagonistic pairs: the triceps contracts to straighten the elbow and in doing so stretches the relaxed biceps.
items.specStatementText: Titin and antagonistic muscles in relaxation
items.random_wrong: Titin in the biceps recoils and pulls its shortened sarcomeres back out, so the triceps is not needed for the movement.

items.q: What is a motor unit in skeletal muscle?
items.correct: One motor neuron and all of the muscle fibres that its branching axon stimulates.
items.misconception: One motor neuron and the single muscle fibre it contacts at one neuromuscular junction.
items.why: Diagrams of the neuromuscular junction show one axon terminal on one fibre for clarity, and the word 'unit' suggests something small and single. The axon of a motor neuron branches to form neuromuscular junctions with many fibres scattered through the muscle. A motor unit is the neuron plus all of those fibres, and they contract together.
items.random_wrong: A whole muscle together with the single motor neuron that stimulates it to contract.

items.q: In a study of two human muscles, a muscle that moves the eye (P) had about 20 000 fibres supplied by 2000 motor neurons, and a calf muscle (Q) had about 1 000 000 fibres supplied by 800 motor neurons. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
items.correct: Force can be increased in smaller steps in P than in Q, because its motor units contain fewer fibres.
items.misconception: Q can be controlled more finely than P, because each of its motor neurons commands a far larger number of fibres.
items.why: 'Better' is equated with 'bigger'. Students also associate control with strength rather than with the size of the smallest step of force available. The size of a motor unit sets the smallest increment of force. Eye muscles have units of around ten fibres; large limb muscles have units of a thousand or more, giving power rather than precision.
items.random_wrong: P produces the more forceful contractions, because its greater number of neurons can send larger impulses.

items.q: A grasshopper's hind leg and a human leg both act as levers moved by muscles. Which comparison is correct?
items.correct: In both, muscles anchored to a rigid skeleton pull across a joint; the grasshopper's attach inside its exoskeleton, the human's to the outside of bones.
items.misconception: In the grasshopper the muscles lie on the outside of the exoskeleton, the reverse of the human arrangement of muscles around bones.
items.why: 'Exo' means outside, and students extend the reversal to everything: if the skeleton is outside the body then the muscles must be outside the skeleton. In both arrangements the muscle pulls on a rigid part across a joint. Arthropod muscles attach to the inside of the cuticle; vertebrate muscles attach to the outside of bones. Both kinds of skeleton provide anchorage and act as levers.
items.specStatementText: Skeletons anchor muscles and act as levers
items.random_wrong: Only the human leg is a true lever, because the grasshopper has no bones and its muscles move the leg without being anchored.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the roles of structures in the human hip joint?
items.correct: Ligaments join the pelvis to the femur and stabilize the joint, and tendons attach the muscles that move it to the bones.
items.misconception: Tendons join the pelvis to the femur and hold the joint together, and ligaments attach the muscles that move it to the bones.
items.why: Both are tough white cords of connective tissue, learned together and hard to tell apart in a diagram, so the labels are swapped. Tendon: muscle to bone. Ligament: bone to bone. At the hip, ligaments hold the head of the femur in the socket of the pelvis, and tendons of the muscles crossing the joint attach to the femur and pelvis.
items.specStatementText: Inside a synovial joint: the hip
items.random_wrong: Cartilage covering the head of the femur secretes the synovial fluid that lubricates the joint and reduces friction.

items.q: A student measures the range of motion of the hip with a goniometer centred on the hip joint, one arm along the trunk and the other along the femur. With the thigh in line with the trunk the reading is 0°. The student flexes the hip as far as possible and records 125°, returns to 0°, then extends the hip backwards as far as possible and records 20°. What is the range of motion of the hip in the flexion–extension dimension?
items.why: 'Range' in mathematics is maximum minus minimum, and students apply the formula to the numbers without picturing where each angle lies relative to the neutral position. Draw the movement. From 20° behind the trunk to 120° in front of it the thigh sweeps through 140°. Treat one direction as negative and the range is still the difference, 120° − (−20°) = 140°.

items.q: Joint angles measured by computer analysis of video images gave these ranges of motion for a volunteer. Hip: flexion 120°, extension 20°, abduction 45°, adduction 30°, medial rotation 40°, lateral rotation 45°. Knee: flexion 135°, extension 0°, abduction and adduction less than 5°, rotation less than 10°. Which conclusion do these data support?
items.correct: The hip moves through useful ranges in three dimensions, whereas the knee moves mainly in one.
items.misconception: The knee is the more mobile of the two joints, because its 135° flexion exceeds any single range at the hip.
items.why: Data comparisons in school are usually one number against another, so students pick the biggest number and ignore that the values belong to different dimensions. Compare range of motion dimension by dimension. The knee flexes about as far as the hip but hardly moves in any other plane; the hip moves usefully in three, which is what a ball-and-socket joint allows.
items.random_wrong: Both joints are hinge joints, because in each the largest range measured lies in the flexion–extension dimension.

items.q: During inhalation the external intercostal muscles contract and move the ribcage up and outwards. What happens to the internal intercostal muscles at the same time, and why?
items.correct: They are stretched, because their fibres run in the opposite direction, and the stretch stores potential energy in their titin.
items.misconception: They contract as well, because the internal intercostal muscles are the layer that moves the ribcage during inhalation.
items.why: The words share a prefix and are learned at the same time, so 'in-ternal' and 'in-hale' become bound together. External for inhalation, internal for forced exhalation. The layers are antagonistic: the orientation of their fibres makes them pull the ribs in opposite directions, and when one contracts it stretches the other.
items.specStatementText: Intercostal muscles: antagonists working inside the body
items.random_wrong: They actively lengthen by pushing, so that the ribs are free to move; a muscle can exert force while lengthening.

items.q: Which example of locomotion is correctly matched with its reason?
items.correct: A male emperor moth flying upwind along the trail of pheromone released by a female: searching for a mate.
items.misconception: A young spider being carried away from its hatching site on a long thread of silk: migration.
items.why: In everyday use a migrant is a person who moves to a new place to live, so 'migration' is taken to mean any relocation rather than a repeated seasonal journey. The examples of migration used in the course are seasonal round trips: Arctic terns, wildebeest and humpback whales all return. Dispersal of young is a different kind of locomotion.
items.random_wrong: A humpback whale swimming from polar feeding grounds to tropical waters where it does not feed: foraging for food.

items.q: How does the way a dolphin propels itself differ from the way a bony fish such as a tuna does?
items.correct: The dolphin's horizontal fluke beats up and down; the tuna's vertical tail fin beats from side to side.
items.misconception: Both tails beat from side to side; the dolphin's fluke is horizontal so that it can also act as a hydroplane.
items.why: Fish are the model for swimming, and a whale silhouette is fish-shaped, so students transfer the fish tail movement without noticing that the fluke lies horizontally. The orientation of the fluke tells you the direction of the stroke: a horizontal blade must beat vertically to push water backwards. This up-and-down flexing of the spine is inherited from land mammal ancestors.
items.random_wrong: The dolphin rows itself along with its flippers, while the tuna's thrust comes from its tail fin.

items.q: A sperm whale can stay submerged for over an hour, then breathes rapidly several times at the surface before diving again. Which adaptation of the airways makes this periodic breathing possible?
items.correct: A blowhole on top of the head that is sealed shut while submerged and opened briefly at the surface.
items.misconception: A blowhole on top of the head through which sea water taken in with food is forced out before each dive.
items.why: The spout looks like a fountain, and cartoons draw whales spouting water; the name 'blowhole' does not say what is blown. The blowhole is the whale's nostrils, moved to the top of the head so that the animal can breathe with only a small part of its body above the surface. It is an airway, not part of the digestive system.
items.random_wrong: An airway that opens into the mouth as well as the blowhole, so that air can be taken in while the whale feeds.

items.q: Which set of features of a dolphin reduces drag as it swims, and so is an adaptation for streamlining?
items.correct: A spindle-shaped body with the hind limbs lost, no external ears, almost no hair and an outline smoothed by a layer of blubber under the skin.
items.misconception: A thick layer of blubber that insulates the body; it makes the outline bulkier, but the extra drag is overcome by the powerful fluke.
items.why: Blubber is met in earlier courses purely as insulation against cold water, and fat is associated with bulk rather than with shape. Streamlining is a property of the whole body outline. Blubber fills in the hollows between skeleton and skin, giving the smooth spindle shape that, together with the loss of hind limbs, external ears and hair, lets water flow past with the least drag.
items.random_wrong: A body made less dense by blubber and large lungs, so that the dolphin floats and does not have to push against the water as it swims.

items.q: Do plants show movement?
items.correct: Yes. Plants do not locomote, but they move parts of the body by differential growth and by reversible changes in cell turgor: shoots grow towards light, sunflower buds track the sun, guard cells open and close stomata, and the leaves of the Venus flytrap snap shut on prey.
items.misconception: Movement requires muscles, so only animals move; plants are alive without moving.
items.why: Movement is often taught as a characteristic of life using animal examples, and checklists of life processes are ticked off with an animal in mind. Muscle is the only movement mechanism most students have studied in detail, so movement and muscle become the same idea. Movement is universal, but the mechanism is not. Animals mostly use muscle; unicellular organisms use cilia, flagella or changes in cell shape; plants use differential growth and reversible turgor changes. The guide asks for the concept of movement to be explored across a range of organisms, including one motile and one sessile species.
items.specStatementText: Movement is universal, locomotion is not
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a barnacle obtain food while cemented to a rock?
items.correct: It actively extends and beats its cirri, feathery legs moved by muscles, to sweep suspended food particles towards its mouth; it is not a passive sieve.
items.misconception: Sessile filter feeders are passive: the water current brings food to them and does all the work, so the organism itself does not need to move.
items.why: Filter feeding is pictured as a sieve held in a current, and sponges, which really do rely on water drawn through them by flagellated cells, are the first sessile animals many students meet. Passive images make it easy to assume that no movement by the animal is involved. Most sessile animals move in order to feed. Barnacles rhythmically extend and beat their cirri; sea anemones and corals move their tentacles; even sponges generate their own current with beating flagella. Movement of parts is an adaptation that lets a sessile organism feed and defend itself without locomotion.
items.specStatementText: Movement is universal, locomotion is not
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an organism show movement only when it travels from place to place?
items.correct: No. Locomotion is one kind of movement; movement also includes moving parts of the body, such as a barnacle beating its cirri, a sea anemone bending its tentacles or a plant leaf closing.
items.misconception: Movement means locomotion: an organism only shows movement when it travels from place to place.
items.why: In everyday language 'to move' usually means to go somewhere, and the topic is titled 'muscle and motility', so students collapse movement into locomotion. They then classify a species as moving or not by whether it has a stage that travels, such as a swimming barnacle larva. Locomotion is movement of the whole organism from place to place; movement is the broader idea and includes movement of body parts. A sessile adult barnacle does not locomote but does move, so it is not an exception to movement being universal.
items.specStatementText: Movement is universal, locomotion is not
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: After a muscle has contracted and shortened, what lengthens it again?
items.correct: An external force, normally contraction of the antagonistic muscle. Titin recoil only returns a sarcomere that has been stretched beyond its resting length; it cannot pull a shortened sarcomere back out.
items.misconception: Titin recoil is what re-lengthens a contracted muscle, so antagonistic muscles are not needed for relaxation.
items.why: Students learn that titin helps sarcomeres 'recoil' and generalize this into a mechanism for returning any muscle to its resting state, treating recoil as the opposite of contraction. Titin is stretched, and stores energy, only when a sarcomere is pulled longer than its resting length. A sarcomere that has shortened by contraction has slack titin and can only be lengthened by a force from outside, which is why antagonistic muscles are needed: muscle tissue can only exert force when it contracts.
items.specStatementText: Titin and antagonistic muscles in relaxation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does titin prevent overstretching?
items.correct: By resisting extension more and more strongly as it is stretched, like a spring that stiffens, so that the sarcomere cannot be pulled to the point where actin and myosin no longer overlap.
items.misconception: Titin prevents overstretching because it is a rigid, inextensible cable between the Z line and the middle of the sarcomere.
items.why: The phrase 'prevents overstretching' suggests something that cannot stretch, and the words 'rope' or 'cable' are used loosely for it. A rigid strut would, however, prevent the sarcomere from being stretched at all and could not recoil. Titin is elastic: it extends readily over the normal range of sarcomere lengths, storing potential energy that drives recoil, and its resistance rises steeply near the limit of that range. It is the combination of elasticity and increasing stiffness that lets it both recoil and prevent overstretching.
items.specStatementText: Titin and antagonistic muscles in relaxation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a motor neuron cause a muscle fibre to contract?
items.correct: Through a neuromuscular junction, a chemical synapse: the neuron releases acetylcholine, which binds to receptors on the fibre membrane and depolarizes it, triggering an action potential in the fibre and release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
items.misconception: The motor neuron is wired directly into the muscle fibre, so its impulse passes straight into the fibre without a synapse.
items.why: Diagrams of the reflex arc show a motor neuron ending on a muscle drawn as a block, and the phrase 'the nerve stimulates the muscle' sounds like an electrical circuit. The synapse between neurons is taught; the one at the muscle is easily overlooked. Each muscle fibre is stimulated at a neuromuscular junction, a chemical synapse using acetylcholine. Neurotransmitter release, receptor binding and depolarization of the muscle fibre membrane come before any calcium ions are released or filaments slide.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where do the calcium ions that trigger contraction of a skeletal muscle fibre come from?
items.correct: From the sarcoplasmic reticulum inside the fibre, which releases stored calcium ions when an action potential spreads over the fibre membrane.
items.misconception: The calcium ions that trigger contraction enter the muscle fibre from the synaptic cleft at the neuromuscular junction.
items.why: Calcium ions appear twice in the story: they enter the presynaptic terminal to trigger release of acetylcholine, and they trigger sliding inside the fibre. Students merge the two events into one flow of calcium from the synapse into the muscle. Calcium entering the motor neuron terminal causes acetylcholine release. Inside the skeletal muscle fibre the trigger for contraction is calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, a store within the fibre, in response to the action potential that acetylcholine initiates.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do myosin heads stay attached to actin throughout a contraction?
items.correct: No. Each head repeatedly attaches, pivots, detaches (when ATP binds) and reattaches further along the actin filament; many heads working out of step keep the filaments sliding smoothly.
items.misconception: Once contraction starts, the myosin heads stay attached and ratchet along the actin filament without letting go, so ATP is needed only once.
items.why: The cycle is often described as myosin 'walking' along actin, and a walker is imagined as always in contact. Animations that show one head pulling can hide that it must release before it can pull again. The cross-bridge cycle is attach, pull, detach, re-cock, reattach, and every cycle uses one ATP. A head pulls only through a short distance per stroke, so a contraction of any size requires each head to cycle many times.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which filament is thick and which is thin?
items.correct: Myosin forms the thick filaments, whose heads project towards the thin filaments of actin. The A band is the length of the myosin filaments; the I band contains only actin.
items.misconception: Actin is the thick filament that carries the heads, and myosin is the thin filament anchored to the Z line.
items.why: The two names are learned as a pair with no obvious link to thickness, and alphabetical order (actin, A band) tempts students to pair actin with the dark A band. Myosin is the motor protein: its molecules bundle into thick filaments with projecting heads. Actin forms thin filaments attached to the Z lines. The dark A band is dark because it contains the thick myosin filaments; the light I band contains only thin actin.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the H zone change width during contraction?
items.correct: Yes. The H zone is the central part of the A band where there is myosin but no actin; as the actin filaments slide inwards it narrows and can disappear.
items.misconception: The H zone is part of the A band, so like the A band it keeps a constant width during contraction.
items.why: Students learn 'the A band stays the same' as a rule and apply it to everything inside the A band, without asking what each region actually contains. Band widths follow from filament content. The A band is the full length of the myosin filaments, so it is constant. The H zone is only the part of the A band not overlapped by actin, so it narrows as overlap increases, just as the I band (actin only) narrows.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a whole muscle controlled as a single unit by one motor neuron?
items.correct: No. A muscle contains many motor units, each with its own motor neuron, and the nervous system varies the force of contraction by recruiting more or fewer of them.
items.misconception: A muscle is one motor unit: one motor neuron controls the whole muscle.
items.why: Reflex arc diagrams in earlier courses show a single motor neuron ending on 'the muscle' as the effector, so a muscle appears to be controlled by one neuron. The motor neuron drawn in a reflex arc stands for many. A muscle such as the biceps contains hundreds of motor units. Recruiting more units produces a stronger contraction, and small units allow fine control.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does the nervous system make a muscle contract more strongly?
items.correct: By recruiting more motor units and by sending impulses at a higher frequency. Action potentials are all-or-nothing, so their size cannot be varied.
items.misconception: A stronger contraction is produced by sending a bigger or stronger nerve impulse down the motor neuron.
items.why: Everyday language speaks of 'a stronger signal', and students meet muscle force before they meet the all-or-nothing nature of the action potential. Every action potential in a motor neuron is the same size. Force is graded by how many motor units are active and how often they fire, which is why a muscle with many small motor units can be controlled so finely.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why do muscles need a skeleton to produce movement?
items.correct: Contraction only produces a useful movement if the muscle is anchored: its ends must be attached to rigid parts so that the pull moves one part relative to another, with the skeleton acting as a lever.
items.misconception: Muscles produce movement on their own; the skeleton is only for support and protection, not for movement.
items.why: The functions of the skeleton are often taught as a list (support, protection, making blood cells) with movement attributed to muscles as a separate system, so the two are not linked. A muscle contracting with nothing to pull against merely changes shape. Skeletons provide anchorage for muscles and act as levers that turn a contraction into movement of the body.
items.specStatementText: Skeletons anchor muscles and act as levers
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the lever formed by the forearm at the elbow, which part is the fulcrum?
items.correct: The elbow joint. The contracting biceps provides the effort where its tendon attaches to the forearm, and the weight of the forearm and anything in the hand is the load.
items.misconception: The muscle is the fulcrum of the lever, or the joint provides the effort.
items.why: Physics lever diagrams show a bar resting on a triangle; mapping the bar, triangle and arrows onto bone, joint and muscle is an unfamiliar step, and students guess. Bone = rigid bar, joint = fulcrum (pivot), muscle pull at the tendon attachment = effort, weight moved = load. The mapping is the same for an arthropod limb and a vertebrate limb.
items.specStatementText: Skeletons anchor muscles and act as levers
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What produces synovial fluid?
items.correct: The synovial membrane lining the joint capsule; the fluid lubricates the joint and nourishes the cartilage.
items.misconception: Synovial fluid is secreted by the cartilage covering the ends of the bones.
items.why: Cartilage and synovial fluid are the two friction-reducing features and sit next to each other in the diagram, so one is assumed to make the other. Cartilage is a smooth, slightly compressible tissue that reduces friction and absorbs shock; it has no blood supply and depends on the synovial fluid, which is secreted by the membrane lining the capsule.
items.specStatementText: Inside a synovial joint: the hip
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In how many dimensions can the hip move?
items.correct: Three: flexion–extension, abduction–adduction and rotation, because the ball-and-socket structure lets the head of the femur turn in any direction within the socket of the pelvis.
items.misconception: The hip, like the knee or elbow, is a hinge that moves in one plane.
items.why: The elbow and knee are the joints used in most textbook diagrams of antagonistic muscles, so a hinge becomes the mental model for every joint. Joint shape determines the dimensions of movement. The hinge joints of the knee and elbow move mainly in one plane; the ball-and-socket hip and shoulder move in three. Range of motion must therefore be compared in several dimensions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A goniometer reads 120° at full hip flexion. Is 120° the range of motion?
items.correct: Only if the starting position was 0°. Range of motion is the difference between the angles at the two extremes of the movement, so both extremes must be measured.
items.misconception: The range of motion is the reading on the goniometer at the end of the movement.
items.why: A single number is easier to record than a difference, and in many school measurements the neutral position happens to read 0°, so the shortcut usually works until it does not. Measure the joint angle at each extreme of the movement in the chosen dimension and find the angle swept between them; if the extremes lie on opposite sides of the neutral position, add the two angles measured from neutral.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If the hip flexes to 125° from the neutral position, can the range in the flexion–extension dimension be found by doubling this?
items.correct: No. Joints do not move equally far on either side of the neutral position: the hip extends only about 20° behind the trunk. Both extremes must be measured separately.
items.misconception: A joint moves equally far on either side of its neutral position, so the range of motion is twice the reading in one direction.
items.why: A door or a hinge in physics swings symmetrically, and measuring one direction and doubling saves a second measurement. Students have rarely checked how far a joint really moves in the less obvious direction. Measure both extremes. At the hip, flexion is large (over 100°) and extension is small (about 20°), so the range in this dimension is their sum, not twice the flexion.

items.q: Why do the two layers of intercostal muscle move the ribcage in opposite directions?
items.correct: Because their fibres run in opposite diagonal directions between the ribs, so contraction of each layer pulls the ribs a different way.
items.misconception: The two layers pull in opposite directions because they are attached to different ribs, or are controlled by different nerves; the direction of the fibres is irrelevant.
items.why: Direction of pull is not something students have had to think about for a muscle drawn as a block; they look for an explanation in what the muscle is attached to rather than in the angle at which it pulls. A muscle pulls along the direction of its fibres. Both layers connect neighbouring ribs, but the fibres of the two layers slope in opposite directions, so shortening of each layer moves the ribs in opposite directions.
items.specStatementText: Intercostal muscles: antagonists working inside the body
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In what form is energy stored in the intercostal layer that is stretched by its antagonist?
items.correct: As elastic potential energy in the extended titin molecules of its sarcomeres, released as the titin recoils when the stretching layer relaxes.
items.misconception: The stretched muscle stores the energy as ATP, ready to power its own contraction.
items.why: 'Energy in a muscle' has always meant ATP or glycogen, so a new statement about stored energy is filed under chemical energy rather than elastic energy. Stretching does not make ATP. It extends titin, a molecular spring, which stores potential energy and recoils, helping the stretched layer return to its resting length and assisting the return movement of the ribcage.
items.specStatementText: Intercostal muscles: antagonists working inside the body

items.q: Do animals only travel in order to find food?
items.correct: No. Locomotion also serves escape from danger, searching for a mate and migration. A humpback whale travels to tropical breeding waters where it does not feed at all.
items.misconception: Every journey an animal makes is ultimately a search for food.
items.why: Energy and food chains dominate earlier ecology teaching, so food becomes the default explanation for any behaviour. The guide lists four reasons for locomotion, each with examples: foraging (a hummingbird visiting flowers), escaping danger (a gazelle fleeing a cheetah), searching for a mate (a male moth flying to a female's pheromone) and migration (the Arctic tern).
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why do wildebeest herds move across the Serengeti each year?
items.correct: To follow the seasonal rains and fresh grazing: it is migration, timed by rainfall and grass growth, not a flight from predators.
items.misconception: Large herds are always on the move mainly to escape predators.
items.why: Wildlife films show predators attacking moving herds, so the movement and the danger become cause and effect in the student's mind. Escape from danger is a short, rapid response, such as a gazelle sprinting from a cheetah. The seasonal movement of a herd is migration, driven by the availability of food and water.

items.q: Are the flippers and fluke of a whale the same kind of structure as the fins of a fish?
items.correct: No. A flipper is a modified forelimb containing the same bones as other mammalian forelimbs (humerus, radius, ulna and digits), shortened and flattened within a paddle; the fluke is a boneless blade of connective tissue at the end of the tail.
items.misconception: Flippers and flukes are fins like those of a fish, unrelated to mammalian limbs.
items.why: Flipper and fin look alike from the outside and do the same job, and the skeleton is rarely shown. Whales evolved from land mammals: the forelimb bones are still present inside the flipper, the hind limbs have been lost, and the fluke is a new structure without bones. In whales and dolphins the flippers are used mainly for steering and stability.

items.q: Can a whale breathe through its mouth?
items.correct: No. In whales and dolphins the airway from the blowhole to the lungs is separated from the mouth and oesophagus, so air enters only through the blowhole and food cannot enter the airway.
items.misconception: Whales can breathe through the mouth as well as the blowhole, as humans can.
items.why: Humans breathe through both mouth and nose, and students assume the mammalian plan is unchanged in whales. The separation of airway and food passage lets a whale feed underwater with its mouth open and still keep water out of its lungs, and lets a large volume of air be exchanged rapidly through the blowhole during brief surfacing between dives.

items.q: Do marine mammals obtain oxygen from the water while they are submerged?
items.correct: No. They breathe air with lungs. Long dives are possible because a large proportion of the lung air is exchanged in each rapid breath at the surface and oxygen is stored in the blood and muscles, not because oxygen is taken from the water.
items.misconception: Marine mammals can extract oxygen from sea water while submerged, which is how they manage such long dives.
items.why: 'Marine' is associated with fish and gills, and dolphins and whales are sometimes called 'fish' in everyday speech. Whales are air-breathing mammals with no gills, and their lungs hold only air. Their adaptations for diving are a closable blowhole on top of the head, a separated airway and a breathing pattern that exchanges a large proportion of the lung air in each brief surfacing; between surfacings they live on oxygen stored in blood and muscle.

items.q: What provides the thrust when a dolphin swims?
items.correct: The up-and-down beat of the fluke, driven by the large muscles of the back and tail; the flippers are used for steering, braking and stability.
items.misconception: The flippers row the dolphin along, like oars, and provide the main thrust.
items.why: Flippers are the visible limbs, and students transfer the way a swimmer's arms or a sea lion's foreflippers work to all marine mammals. In whales and dolphins the limbs are adapted for control rather than power. Propulsion comes from the tail fluke, which is why the muscles of the tail are so large.

items.q: Is the release of calcium ions an essential step between stimulation of a muscle fibre and its contraction?
items.correct: Yes. The action potential that spreads over the fibre membrane does not itself move the filaments: it causes the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release calcium ions, which bind to troponin and shift tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin. Without this step no cross-bridges can form and the fibre does not contract.
items.misconception: The action potential itself makes the filaments slide; calcium ions are a detail, not an essential step.
items.why: The chain 'neuron, impulse, muscle contracts' is learned in earlier courses before the calcium, troponin and tropomyosin step is met, so when calcium ions are introduced they are filed as extra detail in a story that already seemed complete, rather than as the link that makes it work. The impulse and the sliding are connected only through calcium ions. Depolarization of the fibre membrane triggers release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; calcium ions bound to troponin uncover the binding sites on actin; only then can myosin heads attach and pull. If calcium release is blocked, a fully stimulated fibre stays relaxed.

items.q: Does streamlining reduce the effort of swimming by making the animal float?
items.correct: No. Streamlining is a matter of shape: a smooth, tapered body lets water flow past with less drag. Buoyancy is a separate matter and depends on density, not on outline.
items.misconception: A streamlined animal swims easily because it is less dense and floats, so it does not have to push against the water.
items.why: 'Streamlined' is used loosely in everyday speech for anything sleek or light, and students conflate drag, the resistance of water to a body moving through it, with weight or buoyancy. Drag depends on shape and surface, not on density. A marine mammal is streamlined because its body is spindle-shaped with no projecting ears, hind limbs or fur, so the water it moves through is disturbed as little as possible. A floating body still has to push water aside to move forward.
